name: Plumping gloss (menthol / cinnamon)

lead: Plumping glosses give a short-lived, visibly fuller pout without filler. People use them for a quick boost before a photo or night out.

The active ingredients mildly irritate the lip skin, which causes temporary swelling and a tingling or warming feeling. Wikipedia names capsaicin, the compound in chili peppers, as one such ingredient, and menthol and cinnamon are other common ones. The swelling fades within a short time, and no clinical studies of these glosses were found.

paras: People apply the gloss like an ordinary lip product, alone or over lipstick, and reapply for the effect. Results appear within minutes and last a few hours at most.

Because the mechanism is irritation, redness, stinging or discomfort can be expected, and people with sensitive lips or allergies to the ingredients may react more strongly. No studies of adverse events specific to these products were found.

angle.text: Users apply tingling menthol or cinnamon glosses to get a short-lived, visibly fuller pout without filler. Mild irritation causes the lips to swell, and the effect fades. Little formal research covers these specific ingredients.

lead: Plumping gloss, also sold as lip plumper or lifter gloss, is a lip product that makes lips look fuller, smoother and glossier for a few hours. People use it as a quick, non-invasive way to get a fuller lip line without fillers, applied on bare lips or over lipstick. Most formulas add a warming, tingling or cooling sensation on first application, which users take as a sign that the product is working.[1][2]

According to Wikipedia, these products work by irritating the skin of the lips, for example with capsaicin, which causes mild swelling and a temporarily fuller appearance.[2][3] Wikipedia's lip gloss article adds that a similar illusion of fullness can be created with a cooling ingredient such as menthone glycerin acetal.[1] Menthol and cinnamon are the two flavour-and-sensation ingredients most associated with the category. Menthol activates the cold-sensing TRPM8 channel in sensory nerves, and cinnamaldehyde, the main flavour compound of cinnamon, activates the warmth- and irritation-sensing TRPA1 channel.[4][5][6][7]

Wikipedia describes plumping glosses as a cheap and usually harmless alternative to collagen, hyaluronic-acid or fat injections, though less effective because the result is temporary.[1] Plumping gloss sits within the wider lip-gloss market, which Wikipedia notes has grown as lipstick use among young consumers has declined.[1] No clinical studies of irritant plumping glosses were found; the published research concerns the sensory channels their ingredients act on.[4][8]

paras: Lip gloss is a cosmetic that gives lips a glossy lustre and sometimes a subtle colour. It is a mixture of waxes, oils and pigments, with fewer and paler pigments than lipstick, and its main components include lanolin and polybutene.[1] Wikipedia lists the usual formats as wand-applicator tubes, squeezable tubes, roll-ons and semi-solid sticks, and notes that gloss is often used as an introduction to makeup or on occasions when a person wants colour without a heavy lip look.[1]

Plumping versions add ingredients meant to make lips look softer and fuller. Wikipedia's lip plumper entry groups these products with suction devices that cause temporary swelling by drawing blood into the lips, and sets both in a wider history of lip augmentation.[2][9] Wikipedia's consumer-trends section reports that a Lancome gloss line once sold about 20 tubes a minute in the United States and that lip gloss has gained popularity through social media, including lip-gloss keychains and phone cases.[1]

Wikipedia states that plumpers work by irritating lip skin, for example with capsaicin, the compound that gives chili peppers their heat, producing swelling and a temporarily fuller look.[2][9] The capsaicin article describes capsaicin as binding TRPV1 receptors on pain-sensing nerve fibres, producing warmth, tingling or stinging, and reaching the outer skin layer within about a minute.[3]

Menthol-type ingredients act differently. Menthol activates TRPM8, a cold- and menthol-sensing ion channel involved in thermosensation, and Wikipedia's menthol article says it triggers a cooling sensation without changing skin temperature, much as capsaicin triggers heat sensors.[4][6] Products using cooling agents such as menthone glycerin acetal are described as creating an impression of fullness.[1] A pharmacology review of peppermint oil, whose main constituent is menthol, describes a range of biological activities studied in laboratory and clinical settings, mostly outside cosmetics.[10]

Cinnamon flavour in glosses comes from cinnamaldehyde or cinnamon oils. Wikipedia's cinnamaldehyde article describes it as a reactive compound that activates TRPA1, producing the warming or burning sensation associated with cinnamon and similar spices.[5] A pharmacology review describes TRPA1 as a chemical irritant sensor on pain-sensing nerve fibres, present alongside TRPV1 in a subset of those fibres.[7][8] Wikipedia's TRPA1 article lists cinnamaldehyde and mustard oil among its best-known activators and notes that menthol has also been reported to act on it.[8]

A randomised trial of repeated oral capsaicin exposure found that responses to capsaicin fall over time, a process called desensitisation.[11] That study concerned the mouth rather than lip cosmetics, and the capsaicin article describes the same process as the basis for topical capsaicin analgesics.[3]

Product pages and community posts describe plumping glosses by sensation: peppermint or menthol versions that feel cool, cinnamon versions that feel warm, and capsaicin or pepper-extract versions that sting more strongly.[1][3][5][6] Wikipedia notes that gloss can also include fragrances, flavourings and colour additives alongside the active ingredient.[1] Some products pair the irritant with moisturising oils or hyaluronic-acid-labelled ingredients, so the finished gloss also adds shine and a smoother-looking lip surface.[1]

Cinnamon- and menthol-flavoured lip products are also common without any plumping claim, since both are standard flavourings for candy, gum and oral products. Wikipedia lists cinnamaldehyde flavour use in chewing gum, ice cream, candy and beverages.[5]

Wikipedia's lip augmentation article describes a history that runs from unsuccessful paraffin injections around 1900, through liquid silicone from the early 1960s (abandoned about thirty years later over health and long-term appearance concerns) and bovine collagen from about 1980, to fat transfer and hyaluronic-acid fillers after 2000. It places lip plumpers and suction pumps among the non-surgical alternatives, with temporary effects.[9]

The same article lists common and temporary filler effects as redness, swelling, itching and bruising lasting several days to a week, and describes fat grafting as a method for a semi-permanent result. Hyaluronic-acid fillers are described as lasting around six months in the case of Restylane.[2][9] Plumping glosses require no needles or recovery time, and their effect is correspondingly short-lived.[1]

Wikipedia notes that lip glosses are generally considered safe when used as directed, but fragrances, flavourings, preservatives and colour additives can cause allergic reactions or irritation in sensitive people, with redness, dryness, itching or swelling of the lips. Shared applicators can harbour bacteria, and regulators set limits for contaminants such as lead in cosmetics.[1] Because plumping glosses work through irritation, burning or tingling on application is expected.[1][2]

The capsaicin article describes capsaicin as a strong irritant and sensitiser that can cause burning or stinging on skin contact and intense tearing and pain in the eyes.[3] The cinnamaldehyde article lists skin-irritation and skin-sensitisation hazard statements and says allergic contact stomatitis in sensitised people is believed to be uncommon.[5] The menthol article lists skin- and eye-irritation hazard statements.[6]

No studies found for menthol, cinnamon or capsaicin plumping glosses. Laboratory and pharmacology research exists on the sensory channels these ingredients act on, including TRPM8, TRPA1 and TRPV1, and on peppermint oil as a material.[4][7][10]

lore.intro: Plumping gloss is discussed mainly as a consumer beauty product; community posts are about sensation, flavour and how long the swelling lasts.

timeline.event: Surgeons try paraffin injections for lip enhancement, without success, an early step in the lineage of lip augmentation.[9]
Max Factor invents lip gloss for film use.[1]
Max Factor's X-Rated, the first commercially available lip gloss, launches; the original formula was sold until 2003.[1]
Liquid silicone lip augmentation begins and is later abandoned over health and long-term appearance concerns.[9]
Injectable bovine collagen enters the market and becomes the benchmark for later fillers.[9]
Fat transfer and hyaluronic-acid fillers become widely available; temporary plumping glosses and suction pumps are listed as non-injectable alternatives.[2][9]
A review in the Handbook of Experimental Pharmacology summarises TRPM8 as a cold- and menthol-activated thermosensory channel.[4]
A pharmacology review describes TRPA1 as a chemical irritant sensor on pain-sensing nerves.[7]
Lip gloss is reported as the most-searched-for lip care product category on Google in a trend described by Wikipedia, with lip gloss use rising among Gen Z consumers.[1]
A randomised trial reports that repeated low-dose oral capsaicin exposure reduces the response to capsaicin.[11]
